newsitem.title: GERMANY: Italy's Prodi comes to Bonn as EMU pressure rises.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi comes to Bonn as EMU pressure rises.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi arrived in Bonn on Thursday to discuss Europe's single currency with Chancellor Helmut Kohl as German financial figures piled on pressure for a rock-solid economic and monetary union (EMU).

Prodi's visit followed similar talks between Kohl and Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar on Tuesday which also focused on efforts by the two Mediterranean states to qualify for EMU at its planned start in 1999.
Prodi was due to return directly to Rome after the two leaders dined at Kohl's bungalow on the chancellery grounds. A government spokesman said no statement was expected.
Kohl and Prodi posed for photographers before going into the bungalow but declined to answer questions. Kohl advised reporters they would be better off spending their evening enjoying a good meal.
This week's visits by Prodi and Aznar came amid warnings by Germany's central bank, the Bundesbank, against any "window-dressing" to juggle national budgets to meet the stiff criteria for EMU.

Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said membership of Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) was essential for any country wishing to be part of EMU. Italy is not a member of the currency grid but hopes to join soon.
"The (Maastricht) Treaty is very clear on this point. Membership in ERM is a condition," Tietmeyer told Swedish reporters at a press meeting in Frankfurt.
He earlier stressed in an interview with the French daily Le Monde that the European Union would have to look at candidates' long-term economic prospects before accepting them as EMU members.
EU officials say Italy and Spain have slim chances of meeting all the Maastricht treaty requirements for EMU despite their recent efforts to tighten fiscal controls to qualify.
Prodi arrived only hours after a top German commercial banker suggested that southern European nations must be excluded from the first wave of EMU membership to ensure its stability.

"Union must begin with Germany, France, the Benelux nations, Ireland and Austria, but not immediately with the Mediterranean nations," Ulrich Cartellieri, board member of Deutsche Bank AG, Germany's largest commercial bank, said in a speech in Luxembourg.
Kohl's meetings with Aznar and Prodi fuelled speculation about a possible deal for Spain and Italy to join the commmon European currency soon after 1999, an idea some EU officials favour.

Diplomats said Prodi should expect the same as Aznar got -- encouragement to keep trimming budgets to meet the Maastricht convergence criteria but no further public commitment. "It is far too early for Kohl to say anything more," said one envoy.
